pages.title: Variational inference with neural networks, end-to-end

blocks.html: The paper introduces the Variational Autoencoder — a deep generative model that combines an encoder network (which infers a latent distribution from data) with a decoder network (which reconstructs data from a latent sample) — and shows how to train both with a single, fully-differentiable objective using a trick called the reparameterization trick.

The contribution is double: a probabilistic generative model that scales to large datasets, and a recipe for amortized variational inference that broke through what had been a major obstacle in Bayesian deep learning.

Assume data $x$ is generated by an unobserved latent variable $z$: first sample $z \sim p(z)$ (the prior, typically $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$), then sample $x \sim p_\theta(x | z)$ via a neural network (the decoder).
We want to do two things:

items: Generate new samples: easy — sample $z$ from the prior, push through the decoder.
Learn the parameters $\theta$: maximize the data log-likelihood $\log p_\theta(x)$. This requires integrating out $z$: $p_\theta(x) = \int p_\theta(x | z) p(z) dz$. Intractable for neural networks.

blocks.html: Introduce a learned encoder network $q_\phi(z | x)$ that approximates the true posterior $p(z | x)$. Standard variational inference gives a tractable lower bound on the log-likelihood (the ELBO):

items: Reconstruction: how well the decoder reproduces $x$ from a $z$ sampled by the encoder. Maximized by accurate reconstruction.
KL divergence: how close the encoder's posterior is to the prior. Maximized by keeping latents near $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$ — a regularizer that prevents the latent code from memorizing the input.

blocks.html: Amortized inference: instead of running an optimization procedure per datapoint to infer $z$, the encoder learns a single function $x \mapsto q_\phi(z|x)$ that works across all inputs. One forward pass per inference.
The ELBO has an expectation over $q_\phi(z|x)$ — i.e. a sampling step. You can't backprop through a random sample directly: $\partial z / \partial \phi$ is undefined when $z$ is drawn stochastically.

Reparameterization: assume $q_\phi(z|x) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_\phi(x), \sigma_\phi^2(x))$. Then sampling $z \sim q_\phi$ is equivalent to sampling $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ and computing $z = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \cdot \epsilon$. Now $z$ is a deterministic function of $\phi$ given the random draw $\epsilon$ — gradients flow through $\mu$ and $\sigma$ cleanly.

This is the technical kernel of the paper. Without it, the encoder couldn't be trained jointly with the decoder by gradient descent. With it, the whole system becomes an end-to-end-differentiable autoencoder with a probabilistic interpretation.

VAE is benchmarked on MNIST and Frey Faces. Quantitatively it produces competitive log-likelihood (later beaten by other generative models, but a solid baseline in 2013). Qualitatively it generates clean if slightly blurry samples — the Gaussian decoder's mean tends to average across plausible reconstructions.

More important than the numbers: walking through latent space produces smooth interpolations. Two random latents and the path between them generates a smooth morphing through plausible images. This continuous latent structure is exactly what the KL-to-prior term incentivizes.
VAEs were the first practical deep generative model with a continuous latent space and a principled training objective. They opened up:

items: Conditional VAEs (CVAE) — generate conditioned on labels.
Disentangled representations (β-VAE) — encourage independent latent dimensions.
Discrete latents (VQ-VAE) — used in DALL-E, codec models, and the modern audio/image tokenizers underlying multimodal LLMs.
Hierarchical VAEs (NVAE) and the broader 'latent variable model' framework that diffusion models extend.

blocks.html: Modern diffusion models (next paper: DDPM) can be viewed as a deep hierarchical VAE with thousands of latent timesteps and a fixed (rather than learned) inference network. The conceptual lineage runs straight back to this paper.
